title: Every time Diddy changes his name, he washes away a batch of old scandals
dek: Each of Sean Combs's renamings over thirty years was a brand reboot: control the room, control the list, control the narrative, and clear out old scandals one by one — until Cassie Ventura's lawsuit finally couldn't be covered up.
why: This is not a celebrity-downfall recap. It takes apart a liability-shielding mechanism that ran for thirty years: who stayed silent, who benefited, and how even the reporter herself ends up asking whether she was complicit.
who: Readers, journalists and researchers interested in how celebrity power operates; especially suited to anyone trying to understand why, when "everyone knew," no one spoke.
skip: After 42:02 it's a review of a different film, unrelated to this episode — you can skip it.

points.h: Pop culture had been treating it as a joke for years
points.body: More than twenty years before Combs was taken into custody, pop culture was already making fun of his parties and his temper. The host plays two clips: in the 2000 film Scary Movie, Regina Hall's Brenda describes how Puff Daddy's pool party spirals out of control; in a 2008 Mad TV parody of Hannah Montana, P. Diddy films everything on a camera phone. There were earlier warning signs too: a record company executive blacklisted him over his behavior toward women, someone at Howard said they had seen him beat a woman with a belt outside his girlfriend's dorm, and on tour his entourage left behind a stolen handgun. Roundtree's judgment is that this was essentially background noise in the industry — it was just that his spectacle was bigger than every individual incident that surfaced along the timeline, and it covered all the allegations.

points.h: He was the gatekeeper of New York's cultural scene
points.body: Roundtree says that in that period he was simply the gatekeeper of culture in New York. The people who wanted in weren't only music people but power brokers, models, actors; he controlled who got through the door and controlled the atmosphere of the room, so everyone had to court him. She points out in particular that this network was cashable: being able to control the environment and make people ingratiate themselves for access, he later turned those connections into business deals and into that identity of "everyone wants to be around him." And early on all of it was dressed up as "relax, hang out with people in the industry" — it was the later civil suits that reclassified it: the plaintiffs say those occasions were where they were sexually assaulted.

Mosley runs through his 2000s empire — records, clothing, vodka, restaurants, television and film — and notes he follows the same pattern as Trump, whom he openly admired: after every scandal he not only survived but got bigger. Roundtree dates the starting point to the City College incident: a charity basketball game he helped promote to raise money for HIV/AIDS was oversold, a stampede broke out, and nine people died. The investigation found him partly responsible for inadequate security, and he paid a large settlement to the victims' families, but reputationally and career-wise it was "business as usual." She says his success protected him all along — first Uptown Records covered for him because he had already proven his value, and later so did Mary J. Blige's success.

Cassie signed to Bad Boy at 19 and was with Combs for nearly 11 years. Roundtree says the relationship was unconventional: the two never lived together, and she was never included in his family holidays, which was itself a major point of friction between them. She released only one album but signed for nine more. Sources told Roundtree that Cassie was always making music and always wanted to continue her own music career, but Combs would deliberately stall singles and albums, using power over her career as a weapon — when they fought he would say, "Your show is canceled. You're not getting your album. This isn't coming out." After a demo that was supposed to be her follow-up album leaked, The Guardian's review said it would have been album of the year.

points.h: The jury believed the domestic abuse, not the coercion
points.body: The prosecution's core theory was that these hotel sexual encounters constituted sex trafficking because the women were coerced into participating. For Cassie, they argued physical violence was the coercive means of keeping her compliant; for the woman code-named Jane, they argued that financial support was itself coercion. Roundtree thinks coercion is extremely hard to prove. After the verdict a juror came out to explain, and at least one said they believed Cassie's account of domestic abuse but could not prove his intent to coerce them, and that is where the charge stalled. The way Jane entered the case is telling too: she never filed a civil suit; the prosecution found her messages in Combs's texts three days after Cassie sued, and she wrote that it felt like reading her own sexual trauma; before that she had been cooperating with Combs's defense lawyers.

points.h: This is also a workplace story
points.body: Roundtree repeatedly stresses that the prosecution never made this clear: it is also a workplace story, and nearly all the main witnesses had worked for Combs. As employees they were forced to witness domestic abuse, felt threatened themselves, and feared being blacklisted by the industry the moment they spoke. Strip away the lurid shell and it was an environment that pushed employees into the role of personal assistants serving the boss's sex life — supplying drugs, cleaning up humiliating hotel rooms, covering up his domestic abuse of his girlfriend. Their ambitions were to make music and learn the business, but their lives revolved around this. People who tried to report it or leave were fired, pushed out; some say they were pinned against a car hood, shoved out a door, their arm slammed into a wall. She says it is precisely these consequences that produced a culture of silence.

points.h: Without co-conspirators, there is no criminal enterprise
points.body: The government called it a criminal enterprise, but only Combs was charged. His defense lawyer asked in return: if there was a conspiracy, where are the co-conspirators? Roundtree says the absence of co-conspirators testifying is the prosecution's biggest hole. When you hear words like "conspiracy" and "organized racketeering," what comes to mind is the mob, a big organization with big guns; and when the picture is drawn as one man, his assistant, his old bodyguard friend he grew up with, plus a few fresh college graduates as the co-conspirators, it's hard to square the concept of "organized racketeering" with "that's it?" Separately, more than twenty men have also accused Combs of sexual misconduct or assault, but their experiences barely entered the criminal case — Roundtree says that didn't fit the prosecution's working theory.

points.h: The comeback script is already being written
points.body: Combs is expected to be released in early 2028. Roundtree mentions a Netflix documentary produced by 50 Cent that recently won an Emmy for editing; it includes real-time footage from before his September 2024 arrest, as he was planning his own documentary and comeback story. She says this confirms once again that he has always kept tight control of his image, and we should expect the same after his release. There have also been recent reports that he is in touch with someone who does digital communications so he can keep tabs on what social media says about him. Roundtree has no doubt that once out, he will tell these years his own way.
